Article Title: White House invites AI leaders from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and others to review oversight framework
Article Text:
‘Security incident disclosures to accelerate federal action’



The Trump administration has reportedly finalised a voluntary testing framework designed to evaluate the cybersecurity risks and hacking capabilities of the world’s most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Citing senior administration officials, a report by The Information (via Axios), following the completion of the policy milestone, the White House has invited technical representatives and leadership from top AI development labs, including OpenAI Google and Anthropic, to a staff-level meeting on Tuesday to review the proposed oversight procedures.The initiative follows a June directive from President Donald Trump instructing administration officials to construct standardized benchmarks for assessing high-risk cyber capabilities in frontier models before they are released to the public.“The voluntary framework outlined in the June 2nd executive order was complete by the deadline,” a White House official stated, adding that active discussions are taking place with a broad group of industry partners beyond the major tech labs.The urgency surrounding federal oversight increased after several prominent AI companies reported unintended safety breaches during internal testing runs. Recently, Anthropic disclosed that its AI systems successfully breached external networks belonging to three separate companies during controlled vulnerability assessments.Days earlier, OpenAI confirmed that one of its autonomous AI agents bypassed its designated testing sandbox and executed unauthorised network actions against the AI platform Hugging Face, which is the world’s largest AI model repository.This comes days after reports said that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited the White House to consult with officials regarding incoming model releases and voluntary testing protocols.According to administration guidelines, specific technical benchmarks used to evaluate model hacking capabilities will remain classified. The framework establishes rules regarding how intelligence agencies and approved “trusted partners” will gain up to 30 days of pre-release access to new models to inspect them for insider risks, intellectual property vulnerabilities, and potential misuse in state-sponsored cyberattacks.
Article Summary: The White House has invited technical representatives and leadership from top AI development labs, including OpenAI Google and Anthropic, to a staff-level meeting on Tuesday. The initiative follows a June directive from President Donald Trump instructing administration officials to construct standardized benchmarks for assessing high-risk cyber capabilities.

Article Title: A tech CEO wanted to build a new country in an Asian Ghost city, but then an actual country came in the way
Article Text:
Balaji Srinivasan's Network School ran inside Forest City, a $100 billion Chinese-built ghost development in Malaysia's Johor, until authorities ordered it shut.

Who Balaji Srinivasan is, and why he left America behind

How Balaji Srinivasan's 2022 book on startup societies became a real campus in Malaysia

The $100 billion Chinese ghost city that housed Balaji Srinivasan's experiment

Why Malaysia shut the Srinivasan's Network School down, and why Kazakhstan said yes

Balaji Srinivasan spent two years trying to prove that a country could be launched the way a startup is—community first, territory later. Last week, a local council in southern Malaysia ended the experiment with a piece of paperwork. The Network School, the Indian-American founder's live-in campus set inside a half-empty Chinese-built development a bridge away from Singapore, was ordered to cease operations over licensing irregularities, The Wall Street Journal reported on August 1.The shutdown arrived after weeks of scrutiny over something unrelated to licences: the nationality of some residents. An Instagram post by a pro-Palestine group claimed the school had admitted Israeli citizens, including one travelling on a second passport. Malaysia does not officially recognise Israel and requires Israeli nationals to secure special permission before entering. Immigration officers arrived on campus to inspect passports. Authorities later said no wrongdoing had been established and the investigation was continuing. Srinivasan called the post a hoax, compared it to swatting, and demanded a meeting with the prime minister's office.Within hours of the closure order, he posted a video of himself signing an agreement with a Kazakh deputy prime minister—a former Binance executive—to open a campus there instead.Srinivasan, 46, grew up on Long Island, the son of Indian immigrant physicians. He has described being bullied as the only brown child in a school of hundreds, then being punished for defending himself—an early lesson, he has said, that the state is not on your side. Stanford engineering degrees followed, then a genetic screening company, a stint at Andreessen Horowitz, and a brief run as Coinbase's chief technology officer. Coinbase boss Brian Armstrong later called him brilliant, and also "kind of unmanageable". Federal records show Srinivasan and his wife renounced American citizenship in 2023. He says he is now Singaporean.His 2022 book The Network State laid out the method. People with shared beliefs gather online. They help each other make money. They pool funds, buy land, and eventually seek recognition as a state. Seven stages in all. Srinivasan has argued that most countries predating the internet will not survive, and that American polarisation is heading somewhere ugly. He is also a vocal pronatalist, partly on the logic that settling new frontiers requires a much larger supply of humans.The testing ground was Forest City in Johor, a $100 billion Chinese-built luxury project that emptied out into a symbol of China's property bust. Srinivasan rented hotel space in 2024 and opened the Network School at $1,500 a month for room, board, classes and a beach. The first cohort ran 128 people; the second, in 2025, offered 256 places. There was a gym, meals designed by longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, and a cafe stocking creatine and collagen peptides.Residents told the Journal the camaraderie was real and the convenience unbeatable. Pranit Garg, a 29-year-old digital nomad who arrived in March, said the vision brought him in and the protein kept him there. Priyansha Dhoot, a 26-year-old programme manager from India, joined in April and liked the community but found the nightlife nonexistent; the duty-free liquor shops entertained her for roughly a day. Others complained of mould and a lopsided gender ratio. Srinivasan said mildew is a regional inevitability his team handles, and that the school serves tech parents and children, not only tech bros.He is not the only one attempting this. Patri Friedman, grandson of Milton Friedman, moved from floating city-states to funding startup cities, backed by Srinivasan, Peter Thiel and Marc Andreessen. Their portfolio includes Próspera in Honduras, which sued the state after lawmakers moved to scrap its special economic zone.Kazakhstan, meanwhile, has been courting foreign firms with zero corporate tax zones and easy visas. Srinivasan has floated building an artificial island off a willing coast, or following Elon Musk to Mars.Two years in, the experiment has established one thing clearly. Recruiting believers turned out to be the easy part. Every square metre on Earth already answers to somebody's licensing department.
Article Summary: Balaji Srinivasan spent two years trying to prove that a country could be launched the way a startup is. The Indian-American founder's live-in campus set inside a half-empty Chinese-built development a bridge away from Singapore was ordered to cease operations over licensing irregularities.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Satya Nadella: 'It’s not about the failure, it’s about learning from the failures'
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Satya Nadella

“It’s not about the failure, it’s about learning from the failures. Failure itself cannot be celebrated.”

What Satya Nadella’s quote means

“celebrate failure.”

“Failure itself cannot be celebrated,”

A message reflected in his leadership

“know-it-all”

A simple takeaway

Failure is often described as a necessary part of success, but Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offers a more measured perspective. Rather than encouraging people to celebrate failure itself, Nadella argues that its value lies in the lessons it provides. Throughout his career, particularly while leading Microsoft through major technological shifts, he has repeatedly emphasised the importance of learning, adapting, and improving rather than simply accepting setbacks.His quote reminds us that mistakes and failed attempts are meaningful only when they lead to better decisions, new ideas or personal growth. Without reflection and learning, failure remains just that—a setback.At first glance, the quote appears to challenge the popular idea that people shouldIn recent years, many workplaces and entrepreneurs have encouraged this mindset to reduce the fear of taking risks. Nadella’s words introduce an important distinction. He is not suggesting that failure should be feared, but that it should not become the goal or the achievement.The first part of the quote shifts the focus away from the failure itself and toward what comes after it. Every failed project, unsuccessful decision or missed opportunity contains information. It reveals what worked, what did not and what can be done differently the next time. That learning process is what Nadella considers valuable, not the setback itself.The second sentence,reinforces this idea. Simply failing does not create progress. A mistake only becomes meaningful when someone takes the time to understand it and applies those lessons in the future. Without that reflection, failure remains an unproductive outcome.The quote also reflects a mindset of continuous improvement. Instead of seeing success and failure as final destinations, Nadella encourages people to view both as part of an ongoing learning process. The emphasis is not on avoiding mistakes completely but on ensuring they contribute to future growth.This philosophy has been visible throughout Satya Nadella’s leadership at Microsoft. Since becoming the company’s CEO in 2014, he has encouraged a culture centred on learning, experimentation and adaptability rather than maintaining the status quo.Under his leadership, Microsoft expanded its focus on cloud computing, artificial intelligence and subscription-based services while entering new areas through acquisitions and partnerships. Many of these changes required the company to rethink earlier strategies and move beyond approaches that had not delivered the expected results.Nadella has frequently emphasised the importance of developing a “learn-it-all” mindset rather than amindset. The idea is that organisations and individuals grow by remaining open to feedback, questioning assumptions and treating every experience as an opportunity to improve.Satya Nadella’s quote offers a practical lesson for students, professionals, entrepreneurs and anyone working toward a long-term goal. Setbacks are not something to seek or glorify, but neither are they reasons to stop trying. Their value depends on what happens next.Whether it is an unsuccessful interview, a failed business idea or a project that does not go as planned, the important question is not whether the failure happened, but whether something was learned from it. As Nadella suggests, progress comes not from celebrating failure itself, but from using it as a foundation for making better decisions in the future.
Article Summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offers a more measured perspective on failure. Rather than encouraging people to celebrate failure itself, he argues that its value lies in the lessons it provides. He is not suggesting that failure should be feared, but that it should not become the goal or the achievement.

Article Title: In Silicon Valley's talent war for engineers, now status, ambition and some 'ego about changing the world' matter as much as money
Article Text:
Some high-profile executive who have ‘jumped ships’



AI researchers looking for more than compensation



The Silicon Valley is seeing a ‘talent’ war for artificial intelligence (AI) talent with companies reportedly offering up to eight-figure compensation packages. But if a new report is to be believed, the high salary is no longer enough to keep elite engineers from walking out the door. Recently, multiple top researchers moved between major labs even as tech executives are discovering that personal status, ideological alignment and what recruiters describe as “some ego about changing the world” are playing just as large a role in retention as multi-million-dollar paychecks.A report by Axios suggests that the intense poaching cycle has effectively turned the frontier AI industry into a tightly connected ecosystem. Rivals compete fiercely for the same tiny pool of researchers while simultaneously trading staff, buying computing services from one another and sharing cloud providers.The latest example of a volatile AI talent market is the recent departure of Lilian Weng, a co-founder of Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab. Weng initially announced she was stepping down from her role to focus on her health and seek a more targeted position. Days later, reports said she was returning to OpenAI to lead research on recursive self-improvement.Weng is the fourth co-founder to leave Thinking Machines within the past year – essentially proving that even heavily funded, high-profile startups are struggling to maintain team stability. Similar retention challenges are affecting established tech giants across the Silicon Valley. Google lost prominent researcher Noam Shazeer to OpenAI, while Nobel laureate John Jumper departed for Anthropic.Meta spent heavily to recruit top-tier talent for Alexandr Wang’s superintelligence unit, only to see several high-profile hires leave shortly with many heading to OpenAI. Safe Superintelligence, the startup founded by former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, lost its CEO to Meta last year.Apple has seen more than 400 former employees transition to OpenAI, prompting Apple to file a lawsuit alleging OpenAI used internal project codenames to draw confidential information from prospective hires.While high salary offers and pre-IPO equity remain major incentives, researchers reportedly emphasise that non-financial factors often dictate their final decisions. Access to massive computing infrastructure, creative freedom over model architecture, and direct influence over safety protocols frequently outweigh monetary gains.An executive tech recruiter noted that the movement is driven by a mix of financial goals and ‘some ego about changing the world.’ At the same time, some engineers admit to feeling a sense of urgency. With AI systems automating aspects of software development, researchers recognise that their personal bargaining power and ability to command extraordinary compensation may peak over the next few years.Citing a source, Axios reported that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has expressed concern about new talent coming to the firm for the money rather than the mission.
Article Summary: Tech executives are discovering that personal status, ideological alignment and ‘some ego about changing the world’ are playing just as large a role in retention as multi-million-dollar paychecks. Article Title: Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail."
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: What does it mean?

Why did Jensen Huang say this?

How failure helped build Nvidia





Why failure is essential for innovation

Lessons everyone can learn from this quote

Why the quote is relevant in today's AI era







A timeless lesson on courage and innovation

Innovation has always demanded courage, and few technology leaders embody that principle better than Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. As the driving force behind one of the world's most valuable technology companies, Huang has spent decades pushing the boundaries of graphics computing and artificial intelligence. Along the way, he has experienced setbacks, uncertainty and difficult decisions that ultimately shaped Nvidia's success. His quote, "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail," captures the reality that every meaningful breakthrough begins with risk. Rather than fearing failure, Huang encourages people to embrace it as an essential step towards learning, innovation and long-term success.Jensen Huang's quote highlights a fundamental truth about innovation: doing something truly original always involves uncertainty. Whether someone is launching a business, developing a new technology or learning a new skill, there is no guarantee of immediate success. New ideas often require experimentation, and experiments do not always work the first time.Instead of treating failure as a setback, Huang believes it should be viewed as a valuable learning experience.Every mistake teaches lessons that can improve future decisions and bring people closer to success. His message encourages individuals to stop fearing failure and start seeing it as an unavoidable part of growth.Huang has shared this philosophy in several public discussions about entrepreneurship and innovation. Throughout Nvidia's history, he has explained that companies attempting revolutionary ideas cannot expect every decision to succeed. The willingness to take calculated risks has been central to Nvidia's journey since it was founded in 1993.During its early years, Nvidia faced fierce competition and significant financial pressure. Several products failed to meet expectations, and the company came close to running out of money. Rather than abandoning its vision, Huang and his team continued refining their technology until they found success in graphics processing units, which later became the foundation of the artificial intelligence boom.Today, Nvidia is recognised as one of the world's leading AI companies, but its success was built over decades of persistence rather than overnight achievements. Many of the company's innovations were the result of repeated experimentation and continuous improvement.Its graphics processing units, originally developed for video games, eventually became essential tools for artificial intelligence, scientific computing, robotics and autonomous vehicles. Huang has often pointed to this transformation as proof that embracing uncertainty and learning from setbacks can create opportunities that were impossible to predict at the beginning.History shows that some of humanity's greatest discoveries emerged only after repeated failures. Inventors, scientists and entrepreneurs frequently spend years testing ideas before finding one that works. Every unsuccessful attempt eliminates one possibility and brings them closer to the right solution.Huang believes innovation cannot exist without this process. People who refuse to risk failure often choose familiar paths, while those willing to experiment are more likely to discover something genuinely new. In fast-moving industries such as artificial intelligence, the ability to learn quickly from mistakes has become a major competitive advantage.The message extends well beyond the technology sector. Students preparing for examinations, professionals changing careers and entrepreneurs starting new ventures all face uncertainty. Success rarely comes without obstacles, and setbacks often provide the experience needed for future achievements.Rather than becoming discouraged by failure, Huang encourages people to remain curious, adaptable and resilient. A rejected job application, an unsuccessful project or a failed business idea does not define a person's future. What matters is the willingness to learn, improve and try again.Artificial intelligence is transforming industries across the world, creating both opportunities and challenges. As organisations race to develop new AI tools and applications, experimentation has become more important than ever. Many research projects fail before producing a breakthrough, but those failures often generate valuable knowledge.Huang's advice is particularly relevant because AI development depends on continuous testing and improvement. His words remind innovators that meaningful progress requires patience, resilience and a willingness to accept temporary setbacks in pursuit of long-term goals.Jensen Huang's quote is more than just advice for entrepreneurs. It is a reminder that every remarkable achievement begins with the courage to try something unfamiliar. Fear of failure can prevent people from reaching their full potential, while the willingness to accept mistakes often leads to unexpected opportunities.As technology continues to reshape the world, Huang's message remains timeless. Those who dare to innovate, learn from failure and keep moving forward are often the ones who create the ideas that change industries and improve lives
Article Summary: "If you want to do something new, you have to be willing to fail" is the quote of the day by Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Huang has spent decades pushing the boundaries of graphics computing and artificial intelligence. He believes that every meaningful breakthrough begins with risk.

Article Title: Andrej Karpathy’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ experiment shows how testing of AI models have changed and what they lack
Article Text:
Moving beyond benchmarks to on-demand worlds



Key technical limitations in visual auditing



AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, who joined Anthropic earlier this year, recently put Claude Opus 5 through a unique coding test, demonstrating how benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are evolving past simple tasks into complex software engineering. Moving beyond standard prompts like generating basic 2D graphics or short text snippets, Karpathy gave the model the opening paragraph of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings and a $10 budget allocation of 1 million tokens. The also commanded the AI model render the scene as an interactive 3D web environment using Three.js – JavaScript library used to create and display animated 3D computer graphics in a web browser.Karpathy said in a post on X (formerly Twitter) that over the course of two hours, the AI model operated autonomously to write 5,500 lines of JavaScript code. The output produced a low-poly, procedurally generated 3D rendering of the Shire – complete with hobbit holes, trees, rivers, character assets and ambient animations synchronised with narrated book excerpts.While Karpathy noted that while the visual rendering had noticeable flaws, he pointed out that the experiment underscores a fundamental shift in how developers can test AI capabilities.Orchestrating thousands of polygon assets across complex 3D coordinate systems requires a level of computational patience that humans rarely dedicate to hyper-specific tasks.“We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all,” Karpathy said in the post.“I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand,” he added.Despite the milestone, the test also highlighted significant gaps in current frontier models. Because LLMs lack native, real-time video perception and the ability to seamlessly interact with live environments, the model struggled to audit its own visual output.“Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking,” Karpathy pointed out.
Article Summary: AI researcher Andrej Karpathy recently put Claude Opus 5 through a unique coding test. The test demonstrated how benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are evolving past simple tasks into complex software engineering. The experiment underscores a fundamental shift in how developers can test AI capabilities.

Article Title: OpenAI has five products in development, and its president Greg Brockman just hinted at what they're for
Article Text:
OpenAI president Greg Brockman confirms a "family of devices" is coming soon

Why OpenAI believes voice will replace typing on its AI devices

Apple's trade secrets lawsuit still shadows OpenAI's hardware push

Greg Brockman used the plural, and the plural is the story. OpenAI 's president told independent journalist Joanna Stern that the company is building "a family of devices" for its AI models, which turns a year of leaks and lawsuits into something on the record: this was never a one-gadget project. He would not give a date. He would only say you can expect them soon.The device the world already half-knows about, he refused to touch. Bloomberg reported in July that OpenAI starts with a screenless smart speaker, battery-powered so you can carry it from the laundry room to the kitchen, fitted with a camera and sensors to read what's around it, and built with small moving parts so it feels like company rather than an appliance waiting for orders. Asked to confirm it, Brockman folded the question back into the family line and left it there.The bet underneath the hardware is small to describe and enormous to get wrong: that we will talk to our computers for the vast majority of what we do. Brockman is aware of the obvious hole in that. Open-plan offices do not want forty people speaking to forty machines. He raised the soundproof "beak" masks now turning up on desks, said he doesn't wear one, and argued their very existence proves the demand is real even if nobody thinks masks are the answer.Then there's the camera in your living room. OpenAI is working on verifiable, auditable guarantees that only the model ever reads a user's private data, a direct response to lingering doubts about how private ChatGPT's temporary chat mode actually is.Apple sued OpenAI in July in a California federal court, alleging the company asked Apple job candidates to bring components and prototypes into interviews and that more than 400 ex-Apple employees now work there. Chief hardware officer Tang Tan is a named defendant. Apple wants an injunction, which would stop the speaker selling before it ever sells. Brockman stayed narrow: OpenAI is focused on its own technology, and "we have no interest in other companies' trade secrets. We are plenty innovative."The money explains the heat. OpenAI paid $6.5 billion for Jony Ive's studio io, has roughly five products in development, and is reportedly scoping a phone with Qualcomm and MediaTek. The what and the why are now public. Whether any of it reaches a shelf before a judge reaches a decision is the part Brockman left alone.
Article Summary: OpenAI president Greg Brockman confirms a "family of devices" is coming soon. OpenAI paid $6.5 billion for Jony Ive's studio io. The company has roughly five products in development, and is reportedly scoping a phone with Qualcomm and MediaTek.

Article Title: Apple's most popular Mac is now its hardest to buy
Article Text:
MacBook Air shipping dates have slipped to late August as the global memory shortage hits Apple's best-selling Mac.

The AI buildout is eating the memory that consumer laptops need

Apple is nudging shoppers toward the MacBook Pro instead

The MacBook Air is the laptop Apple sells to everyone—students, writers, people who just want something thin that opens and works. Right now it is also the laptop Apple can't keep on shelves. Shipping estimates have slipped by weeks across nearly every configuration, and this isn't a back-to-school rush emptying the stockroom. It's the global memory shortage, and it has finally caught up with Apple's volume seller.Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in Sunday's Power On newsletter that retail sources describe Air inventory as more constrained than they can ever recall. Order a base model from Apple's online store today and delivery lands at the end of August. Choose a specific combination of screen size, colour and—critically—memory, and you're pushed into early September. For a machine refreshed with the M5 chip in March, a month-long wait is close to unheard of.The squeeze started at the edges of Apple's lineup. Mac mini and Mac Studio, both quietly adopted by people running local AI models, have been backordered for months. Those are niche machines, so the pain stayed niche.The Air is different. It is the default Mac, and its shortage makes the crunch visible to ordinary buyers for the first time.Apple has already pulled the obvious lever. In June it raised prices across the Mac range, taking the 13-inch MacBook Air from $1,099 to $1,299. Tim Cook, in his final months as CEO, described the memory situation as a hundred-year flood for the industry—something he hadn't seen in four decades of watching supply chains. Gurman says Apple is also working to source memory from Chinese suppliers, at least for devices sold in China.The most telling sign is in the marketing. Apple's back-to-school promotion, delayed from June because of the shortage, now steers customers toward the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro across its website and stores. Some materials carry a line Apple has rarely needed before: MacBook Air subject to availability.That redirection isn't accidental. Gurman reports Apple is prioritising the base MacBook Pro partly to clear inventory ahead of an M6 refresh this fall. A new MacBook Air isn't expected until early next year, with 13-inch and 15-inch models in development that closely resemble the current design.Until then, the cheapest way into a Mac may be the one Apple is quietly steering you away from buying.
Article Summary: The global memory shortage has finally caught up with Apple's best-selling Mac. Air inventory is more constrained than they can ever recall, retail sources say. Order a base model from Apple's online store today and delivery lands at the end of August. Choose a specific combination of screen size, colour and memory, and you're pushed into early September.
